data.headline: Paramount CEO Ellison unveils sweeping plan for Warner Bros
data.summary: STORY: Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison unveiled his plans for Warner Bros Discovery on Monday, after clinching a deal to acquire the media giant.On a call with analysts, Ellison said the combined company will have a net debt load of about $79 billion.He ruled out any plans to divest or spinoff Warner Bros' cable TV networks, which include CNN and HBO.Instead, the merger will unite them with Paramount TV assets CBS, MTV, Comedy Central and BET.As for the two companies' streaming services, which include Paramount+ and HBO Max, Ellison said those will be folded into a single streaming platform.:: NetflixHe noted that Paramount and Warner Bros already serve more than 200 million streaming customers, giving them the scale and firepower to better compete with industry leader Netflix.Paramount signed the $110 billion deal for Warner Bros on Friday after a months-long battle with rival bidder Netflix, which declined to raise its offer.Paramount also paid the $2.8 billion termination fee that Warner Bros owed Netflix.The Paramount-Warner deal is expected to close in the third quarter of this year.Ellison's father, billionaire Larry Ellison, has deep ties to the Trump administration, a factor some analysts said could help it secure more favorable regulatory treatment.

data.headline: Moody’s Puts Paramount on Review for Downgrade to Junk
data.summary: Moody's Investors Services said Friday it is placing Paramount Global on review for a downgrade following parent company, Paramount Skydance's winning bid to buy to Warner Bros. Discovery.  Paramount Global carried Moody's lowest investment grade rating of Baa3 so a downgrade would push the company into speculative grade territory, or "junk" status.  Moody's said that while buying Warner Bros. will improve margins and add revenue diversity for Paramount Skydance, it will also "materially increase" leverage and complexity in the company's debt load.

data.headline: Paramount Is Officially Buying Warner Bros. It’s a Victory for Shareholders.
data.summary: Paramount Skydance  investors are set to get a fairy tale ending, with the CBS owner winning the  Warner Bros. Discovery  bidding war.  The companies announced late Friday that Paramount would pay $31 per share in cash for Warner Bros. stock.  It’s a great outcome for Paramount, which only had to raise its hostile tender offer by $1 a share to avoid a prolonged bidding war.

data.headline: Paramount-Warner deal doesn’t signal broader M&A pickup, advisor says
data.summary: STORY: Warner Bros Discovery has agreed to be acquired by Paramount Skydance in a $110 billion deal signed Friday morning, according to an audio clip of a global townhall by the company, which was reviewed by Reuters.The agreement caps a bidding war after Netflix declined to match Paramount's latest $31-per-share offer, which was deemed superior by Warner Bros to the streaming pioneer's $27.75-per-share agreement for its studio and streaming assets.Betz's advice for investors? Focus on economic data and corporate earnings when making investment decisions rather than betting on more M&A deals. "Yes, I know the [Trump] administration seems more friendly in this space with favoring less regulation," he said. data.headline: Netflix surges as investors cheer exit from Warner Bros race
data.summary: STORY: Shares of Netflix jumped as much as eleven-and-a-half percent on Friday, as investors applauded its decision to exit the race for Warner Bros Discovery after a months-long bidding war with Paramount Skydance.Shares of David Ellison's Paramount, meanwhile, soared more than 20%, as a merger with Warner Bros would allow it to tap into some of Hollywood's most prized assets across film, TV and streaming.Netflix declined to match Paramount's latest $31 per share bid, or raise its offer of nearly $28 a share, saying the deal was, quote, "no longer financially attractive.""We were supporting Paramount because we believe in David Ellison..."Tim Richards, founder and chief executive of privately held cinema operator Vue International, said he supported Paramount's bid of Warner Bros because he viewed it as more likely to prioritize theatrical releases than streaming giant Netflix."I'm hoping that Netflix now having really gone in and seen and learned more about how important it is to get a theatrical release, how we are that engine that drives all the ancillary revenue streams, and it's not something to fear, it’s something to embrace, and I'm hoping that some good will come out of that, because we would love to show some of Netflix's amazing movies.”As for Paramount's streaming unit, a combination with HBO Max and Discovery+ would reshape its position in a streaming era long dominated by Netflix.Still, one analyst told Reuters that given Warner Bros' debt load, Paramount's acquisition was, quote, "more about Ellison taking over Hollywood and ego than it is about good business sense."
